name: Treaty with the Wyandot, etc., 1805 (Treaty of Fort Industry)
nations: Ottawa (Odawa) bands of the Maumee, Blanchard's Fork, Auglaize and Roche de Boeuf (Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma)
promises: A new boundary: a meridian line 120 miles west of Pennsylvania, with the land east of it ceded (Articles 2 and 3).

A permanent annuity of $1,000 a year to the Wyandot, Munsee and Delaware, and the Shawnee and Seneca living with the Wyandot, paid at Detroit or another convenient place, $175 of it secured from the Connecticut Land Company (Article 4).
For the Ottawa, Chippewa and Huron River Potawatomi, $4,000 paid and a further $12,000 secured in trust with the President, payable in six annual instalments (Article 5).
The nations could hunt and fish on the ceded land so long as they remained peaceable (Article 6).

breaches.what: The Indian Claims Commission valued Royce Areas 53 and 54, 2,589,807 acres in north-central Ohio, at $1.10 an acre or $2,848,787.70 on 4 July 1805, found the total consideration was $32,666.65, and held that consideration so grossly inadequate as to be unconscionable. Each of the five tribes held an undivided one-fifth interest.

landTaken: Royce Areas 53 and 54, 2,589,807 acres in north-central Ohio, bounded by Lake Erie, the Cuyahoga and Tuscarawas Rivers and the Greeneville Treaty line (Commission opinion of 1978). Area 53 lay within the Connecticut Western Reserve.
compensation: Consideration of $32,666.65 (Commission finding). Net awards set in 1978: Wyandot $561,424.21, Delaware $561,424.21, Chippewa $563,624.21, Ottawa $563,624.21, Potawatomi and intervenors $566,024.21, less offsets. Final awards entered 17 August 1978 for the Potawatomi, Ottawa and Wyandot.
today: The Commission's title decision (30 Ind. Cl. Comm. 8, 1973) was affirmed by the Court of Claims in 1975 (207 Ct. Cl. 958) and certiorari was denied, as recited in the 1978 opinion. Whether the Delaware and Chippewa shares were paid as final awards was not traced.

nationVoice.summary: The Nation's history says the Wyandot, long tied to the French at Detroit, settled Upper Sandusky in Ohio, and that pressure from settlers forced the treaty it dates to 1843 and removal west of the Mississippi, leaving the Wyandot the last tribe to leave Ohio, in July 1843.

The Tribe says that after signing the first treaty with the new United States in 1778 its ancestors had to keep giving up their lands and moving west, to Ohio, then Indiana, Missouri and Kansas and at last Indian Territory, and that its people understood many early land sales as something closer to leases.

openQuestions: Final awards for the Delaware (Dockets 27-E and 202) and Chippewa (Docket 13-E) shares were not found; Docket 13-E was certified to the Court of Claims on 29 September 1978 according to the Commission index, which was not opened.
No statement by a present-day nation about this treaty was found in the time available.

plain.promised: In return for land in north-central Ohio, the United States promised a permanent $1,000 a year to some nations, $4,000 plus $12,000 in instalments to others, and the right to hunt and fish on the ceded land while at peace.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1978 that the 2,589,807 acres ceded were worth $2,848,787.70, that the tribes received $32,666.65, and that this was so grossly inadequate as to be unconscionable.
plain.today: In 1978 the Commission entered final awards for the Potawatomi ($566,024.21), Ottawa ($563,624.21) and Wyandot ($561,424.21). Whether the Delaware and Chippewa shares were paid has not been traced.
